The beta strength function, $g(E_\beta)$, is a critical nuclear structure parameter that characterizes the transition probability for beta decay. This study employs a relativistic mean-field framework to investigate its energy dependence, specifically for the beta decay of $^{130}$Ba into $^{130}$Cs. Our findings indicate that the calculated beta strength is governed by the structural configurations of both the parent and daughter nuclei. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the relativistic mean-field approach accurately reproduces the experimentally measured beta strength distribution.

We introduce a minimal extension to the Standard Model featuring a complex scalar doublet, a real scalar singlet, and right-handed neutrinos. This framework addresses the dark matter problem through a mixed-doublet scenario, where the scalar sector's parameters are tightly constrained by the observed Higgs mass, Higgs coupling strengths, and electroweak precision observables. The model's Higgs spectrum is highly constrained, allowing only a single physical scalar to exist. Consequently, the dark matter candidate comprises both dark matter scalar components and right-handed neutrinos, with their relative abundances jointly satisfying the observed relic density. Furthermore, the right-handed neutrino sector offers a viable mechanism for leptogenesis, providing a potential origin for matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe.

This paper introduces a learning-based control algorithm that leverages a pre-trained generative model to handle disturbances in control systems. The proposed approach consists of two phases: first, a generative model is trained offline on a fixed dataset; second, a control policy is learned online using only a minimal number of interaction steps. Theoretically, the approach is grounded in the concept of distributional shift, which facilitates the transfer of knowledge from offline to online settings. Empirical evaluations on linear quadratic regulators with disturbances demonstrate that the algorithm significantly surpasses traditional reinforcement learning methods, particularly in scenarios constrained by limited data. Furthermore, the paper provides a theoretical analysis of the policy's performance under specific assumptions regarding the generative model.

We establish that the three-point correlation functions of higher-spin currents in Toda conformal field theories satisfy specific spin-three Ward identities, which we derive using the formalism of higher-spin algebras. These algebras, which generalize the $W$-algebras associated with $W$-CFTs, are constructed from the symmetry generators of the differential equations obeyed by the Toda CFT's fundamental fields. Our findings demonstrate that the resulting Ward identities in Toda CFTs extend those of $W$-CFTs, a relationship mediated by the corresponding higher-spin algebras. Furthermore, we show that the differential equations for Toda CFT primary fields, and thus the structure of the higher-spin algebras themselves, can be derived from the operator product expansions of higher-spin currents.

Adversarial Generative Models (GANs) are a potent tool for generating images, yet their training remains notoriously difficult. While recent research has focused on enhancing image quality, this work investigates the impact of varying dataset sizes on GAN performance. We introduce a novel architecture called relation networks (RGANs), which integrate semantic information into image generation. RGANs function by identifying and connecting similar images within a memory bank, allowing the generator to produce new images by leveraging features from the entire collection. Our approach demonstrates significant improvements in image quality, particularly for smaller datasets, and achieves state-of-the-art results on the CIFAR-10 benchmark.

This paper introduces a twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) scheme that employs reference frames to facilitate global phase reference alignment. By utilizing a specific type of phase locking, the proposed TF-QKD scheme achieves higher transmission rates than standard TF-QKD. Furthermore, the scheme's performance is evaluated through both numerical simulations and experimental verification.
This paper examines the symbol spaces of Toeplitz operators acting on $p$-Bergman and $p$-Fock spaces, where $1 < p < \infty$.

Object detection performance relies heavily on the quality of training data, yet manual annotation is costly and time-consuming. This paper introduces a method to automatically generate pseudo bounding-box annotations for images, thereby enhancing object detection models. Our approach consists of two stages: first, a classifier trained on existing bounding-box labels identifies image regions likely to contain objects; second, a segmentation model processes these classified regions to produce the final refined boxes. We evaluated this pipeline on the Pascal VOC dataset using ResNet-50 and a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for detection tasks. Results indicate that our method surpasses annotations created by the COCO dataset, achieving a 2.5% improvement in mean Average Precision (mAP) over the baseline.

Self-absorption in the 21 cm line of neutral hydrogen (HI) and the fine-structure lines of ionized carbon (CII) and ionized oxygen (OI) offers a valuable probe into the physical conditions of the interstellar medium. This study investigates the impact of self-absorption on spectral observations within a star-forming region, utilizing data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Green Bank Telescope (GBT). The observations target the L1641/N1592 complex, a site of active star formation in the Perseus molecular cloud, where a young stellar object (YSO) cluster is forming. The CII and OI emission maps were derived using a two-component model that accounts for both the cold interstellar medium (ISM) and the warm interstellar medium (WISM). The CII and OI line ratios indicate that the WISM is optically thick, whereas the cold ISM remains optically thin. The WISM is identified as a warm, diffuse phase of the interstellar medium, with a temperature of approximately 100 K and a density of $10^3$ cm$^{-3}$. The study also reveals that the self-absorption of HI and CII/OI lines is significantly influenced by nearby stars, a phenomenon that must be considered when interpreting spectral data.

Convolutional networks have long been favored for image classification due to their inductive biases that align with the spatial structure of images. In contrast, Transformer models have gained significant attention for their ability to handle sequential data, prompting researchers to adapt them for image tasks. This study evaluates the performance of Transformers on image classification, comparing them against convolutional networks and addressing the following questions: Do Transformers offer genuine advantages for images? Can their effectiveness be improved? What are the primary limitations? We introduce a new architecture, the Vision Transformer (ViT), which applies the Transformer concept to images by treating patches as input tokens. Our experiments on the ImageNet dataset demonstrate that ViT achieves state-of-the-art results, surpassing conventional convolutional networks. Furthermore, we observe that scaling up the model size yields substantial performance gains, a phenomenon explained by the capacity of large-scale self-attention mechanisms to effectively capture long-range dependencies.

Although classical models for mortality forecasting typically assume time-invariant factor loadings, recent research demonstrates that allowing these loadings to evolve over time can significantly enhance forecast accuracy. This study introduces a Bayesian framework designed to estimate time-varying factor loadages alongside common factors and specific residuals. The model employs a dynamic factor structure where loadages fluctuate according to a Gaussian random walk, utilizing a Bayesian hierarchical framework for the prior distribution of these factor dynamics. The posterior distribution is approximated using a combination of the Kalman filter and Kalman smoothers. The methodology is tested on both synthetic data and real-world mortality records across 12 countries, with results indicating that this approach generates more precise forecasts than traditional single-factor and multivariate factor models.

This study introduces novel techniques to counter interference during Neural Architecture Search (NAS), a process where the evaluation of candidate architectures can be compromised by suboptimal parent models. To address this, we developed two methods: first, a regularization approach that constrains the search space to architectures similar to the parent model, and second, a cross-architecture transfer learning strategy that trains separate classifiers for different architecture families. Evaluations on the CIFAR-10 dataset using the ENAS algorithm demonstrate that these methods enhance performance by 0.5% to 1.0% over both RoBERTa and ELECTRa baseline models. Furthermore, applying the techniques across multiple datasets and algorithms confirms their generalizability and effectiveness.

Time-series feature extraction is a critical step in machine learning pipelines, yet existing tools often fail to accommodate the diverse characteristics of various time-series datasets. To address this limitation, we introduce "stealth," a Python package designed to extract time-series features efficiently. By leveraging a modular architecture, "stealth" allows users to customize feature extraction workflows to suit specific data types. The system integrates with scikit-learn and pandas, ensuring seamless compatibility with broader data science ecosystems. To demonstrate its utility, we apply "stealth" to the Kaggle Store Sales Prediction competition, outlining a complete end-to-end modeling workflow.

We demonstrate that for proper geodesic completeness in locally compact CAT(0) spaces is equivalent to the property of having a finitely generated fundamental group. Additionally, we provide a criterion for determining when a CAT(0) space is geodetically complete by utilizing the topology of its visual boundary.

Translation quality assessment (TQA) is a critical component of the localization workflow, involving a human evaluation of translated content. This process typically relies on the collaborative input of translators and client-appointed reviewers. While current research has extensively examined the impact of reviewers on the assessment outcome, the role of the translator remains largely overlooked. This study addresses this gap by investigating how translator competence influences TQA results. We propose a novel approach that integrates both translator and reviewer profiles to predict quality scores. To achieve this, we introduce a multi-view graph convolutional network (MVGCN) designed to synthesize information from diverse data sources. Specifically, we construct a multi-view graph where nodes represent individual contributors (translators and reviewers), and edges reflect their collaborative interactions. These connections are weighted by the translator's performance metrics and the strength of the reviewer-translator relationship. Furthermore, we incorporate a multi-view fusion module capable of harmonizing data from various sources to enhance the model's predictive accuracy. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing baselines, confirming the significant value of incorporating reviewer and translator profiles within the assessment framework.

We introduce a new approach to determine the eigenchannels of a wave system, grounded in the observation that their intensity profiles correspond to the eigenvectors of a specific matrix. This method is demonstrated using a multiple-slit diffraction setup, where the results align perfectly with those obtained from traditional analytical techniques.

Neural networks have achieved remarkable success across numerous visual tasks, yet their substantial computational requirements hinder practical deployment. While prior research has largely concentrated on model compression and acceleration, this study introduces an innovative pruning strategy called Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP). Unlike previous methods, IMP iteratively refines pruning decisions to achieve more effective compression. Experiments conducted on various CNN architectures across multiple datasets demonstrate that IMP can reduce network size by up to 99% with minimal impact on accuracy. Furthermore, the method is versatile, successfully applying to diverse tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and image classification.

Although the lottery is frequently cited as a mechanism for wealth redistribution, this study demonstrates that it functions more accurately as a tax on the desire for riches. We establish that when ticket prices remain constant, the system yields positive returns for players only when jackpots exceed approximately \$100 million, a threshold that fluctuates based on the specific game format. Conversely, if the jackpot size is fixed, players can achieve positive returns by drastically increasing ticket volume, though this requires coordination among a vast majority of participants. Ultimately, our findings indicate that lotteries serve as a revenue source for governments, benefiting them at the direct expense of their citizens.

We have conducted a comprehensive large-charge expansion for the $O(2)$ non-linear sigma model in both two and four dimensions, deriving the first few terms of the epsilon series for the beta function, critical exponents, and the renormalization group flow of the dimensionless charge. These findings align closely with estimates from Monte-Carlo simulations and perturbation theory. Additionally, we examine the behavior of the renormalization group trajectory in the two-dimensional model with a massive term, demonstrating that the charge flows toward a fixed point characterized by a non-zero value.

Valley Hall transport in graphene is typically attributed to nonuniform strain. However, this study demonstrates that even uniform strain can drive such transport, provided a specific condition is met: the valley-dependent Berry curvature must remain spatially nonuniform. This occurs when a valley-dependent effective magnetic field arises from nonuniform strain, rendering the Berry curvature position-dependent. Consequently, a transverse valley-dependent force emerges in the presence of an electric field, leading to valley-selective transverse currents. This mechanism is experimentally observable in twisted bilayer graphene, where a tunable valley-dependent Berry curvature allows strain-induced valley Hall transport to be regulated via the twist angle.

Model ensembles are well-established for their ability to enhance generalization, yet their application in domain adaptive (DA) settings is limited by the prohibitive memory costs required to store multiple adapted models. To address this, we introduce "model soup," a new scheme that merges the outputs of several DA models into a single unified model. This approach is conceptually straightforward and computationally efficient, requiring minimal overhead. Empirical results indicate that model soup not only matches but often surpasses the generalization capabilities of individual ensemble members. Furthermore, we have developed a specialized variant of model soup that yields additional gains. Collectively, these findings suggest that model ensembles can be effectively realized through model soup without the burden of excessive memory usage.

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a prevalent algorithm for visualizing high-dimensional data via two-dimensional scatter plots. Its success stems from utilizing a Gaussian distribution to model local proximity and a Gaussian distribution for proximity within the embedded space. However, for spherical datasets, the Gaussian distribution fails to accurately capture local relationships. This study proposes replacing the Gaussian distribution in the high-dimensional space with a Cauchy distribution, thereby introducing a new algorithm called t-SNE-C. Comparative evaluations demonstrate that t-SNE-C outperforms standard t-SNE in visualizing both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We have conducted a diagrammatic calculation of the polaron $Z$ factor for a heavy impurity situated within a two-dimensional Fermi sea, utilizing a contact interaction. Our findings indicate that the $Z$ factor derived from the full diagrammatic series aligns remarkably well with the one-particle-hole contribution across all interaction strengths, a result that holds regardless of the impurity's mass. This strong agreement persists even in the strong-coupling limit, where the polaron exhibits a bound state. These conclusions are corroborated by Monte Carlo simulations, which demonstrate that the diagrammatic series converges with impressive speed.

The digital-analog approach to quantum computation merges the strengths of both paradigms: it leverages the flexibility of gate-based digital methods while utilizing the efficiency of analog simulations, which require fewer gates and lower error susceptibility. This hybrid technique is applied to the simulation of the Fermi-Hubbard model, a highly complex many-body system of significant physical relevance. By employing a tailored digital pre- and post-processing alongside a specific analog evolution, the approach generates a Hamiltonian that closely approximates the original model. This resulting effective Hamiltonian captures the essential physics of the system, thereby enabling the study of its fundamental properties.

This paper investigates the matching polynomials of graphs within a family that includes complete graphs, complete bipartite graphs, and their near-misses. Specifically, we identify characterizations for graphs whose matching polynomials match those of complete graphs or complete bipartite graphs. Additionally, we establish a unique polynomial factor for graphs with exactly two non-matching terms and explore the relationship between a graph's matching polynomial and its complement's matching complement.
We demonstrate that quantum pseudo-Anosov representations are closely linked to pseudo-Anosov elements within the mapping class group.

The rapid adoption of Scrum has driven a surge in research examining its impact on project success. However, the majority of these studies focus on general contexts, neglecting the specific challenges and opportunities presented by remote work environments. This paper addresses that gap by investigating the influence of Scrum on project outcomes within remote settings. To achieve this, the authors conducted a systematic literature review utilizing a PRISMA-inspired methodology. The findings indicate that the vast majority of examined studies report a positive correlation between Scrum implementation and success when teams operate remotely. Furthermore, the research identifies key Scrum practices that foster success in this context, including the use of video conferencing for daily stand-ups, the application of collaborative online tools, and the establishment of a virtual co-location environment.
This paper investigates the relationship between the Gau–Wu number of arrowhead matrices and the Gau–Wu numbers of specific associated matrices.

The lifetimes of beauty and charm hadrons are vital parameters for understanding the Standard Model and are essential for analyzing $B$ and $D$ meson decays. This study examines the distributions of impact parameters for beauty and charm hadrons, alongside other background sources, using $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb detector at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The analysis focuses on beauty and charm hadrons, as well as light-flavor particles, within jets that have undergone specific selection criteria. The findings indicate that beauty hadron proper decay lengths are comparable to those of charm hadrons and significantly exceed those of other backgrounds. The study reports measurements of the mean proper decay lengths for beauty and charm hadrons, along with their ratios, across a wide range of jet transverse momenta.

This paper introduces a novel approach to analyzing color interactions within a dataset by employing a new colored persistence homology framework. We propose a specific R-module structure for a dataset's matrix representation, which enables the definition of a corresponding chain complex over persistent modules. By utilizing this construction, we can apply standard persistent homology techniques to calculate topological features of the colored space. These invariants effectively quantify interactions between different color classes. We demonstrate the practical application of this framework through an analysis of a two-dimensional molecular dynamics simulation.

This study investigates the performance of binary power control within large-scale interference networks. We propose a binary scheme that assigns each user to either a high or low power tier, with the specific power level determined by the user's location. We demonstrate that, in large networks, the throughput achieved by optimal power control and this binary variant are asymptotically equivalent. Furthermore, we show that binary power control remains effective in networks with a finite number of users.

The increasing adoption of electronic accounting systems has created opportunities for data mining and machine learning to support auditing. This study introduces a methodology that integrates data mining and machine learning techniques with the Dempster-Shafer theory of evidence to enhance the auditing process. Within this framework, Dempsher-Shafer mass functions are utilized to model the varying levels of interest financial accounts hold for auditors. The approach involves a two-phase process: first, a Bayesian neural network trains on transaction data to generate a Dempsher-Shafer belief rule base, and second, a belief rule-based network is constructed using this information to forecast account balances. The accuracy of these predictions is then evaluated against actual account balances.

This paper presents a novel, efficient method for simulating point processes, termed "Acceptance Rejection Stitching." The approach involves conditioning on a specific event and simulating the point process within the enlarged domain. To address cases where the conditional simulation may fall short of covering the full area, we employ an acceptance-rejection technique to filter points outside the target region. Furthermore, we utilize stitching to merge multiple such accepted simulations, ensuring complete coverage of the domain. The study provides rigorous mathematical proofs demonstrating that this method accurately reproduces the point process. We illustrate the approach with simulations of a Matérn cluster process and a Matérn Cox process, which are widely recognized models in spatial statistics.

This study examines the deformation of Galilean transformations within the framework of the Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUS). Our findings indicate that the resulting deformed Galilean transformations are mathematically analogous to the Lorentz transformations, albeit with the velocity of light substituted by the Planck constant. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the deformed Doppler shift in this context is equivalent to the relativistic Doppler shift.

Scheduling in multitasking systems is a well-established research area, yet it has primarily focused on discrete, fixed processing shares. This paper introduces a novel scheduling framework that enables processors to be shared among tasks via continuous, variable ratios. We propose a new algorithm, $\epsilon$-Share, which dynamically adjusts these sharing rates to achieve optimal scheduling outcomes. Our findings demonstrate that $\epsilon$-Share is $\rho$-competitive for any $\rho > 1$, whereas no online algorithm can achieve a finite competitive ratio for general cases. Additionally, we show that the algorithm's performance is highly sensitive to the distribution of sharing ratios among tasks.

This study introduces a feedback control strategy for legged robots traversing deformable surfaces, accounting for both surface deformation and hysteresis effects. By employing a nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) framework, the method generates a sequence of control inputs to accurately follow a predefined trajectory. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances trajectory tracking performance compared to open-loop control. Furthermore, the control scheme enables robots to hop over soft ground with a size comparable to their own body, a feat unachievable without feedback. Finally, the paper outlines a methodology for developing and validating a soft-ground simulation model using experimental data.

Over-the-air (OTA) updates are essential for managing large-scale IoT deployments, yet they face significant challenges due to prolonged transmission times and the risk of data corruption. While concurrent transmissions (CT) have previously been shown to accelerate single-user updates, their viability for multi-user scenarios remains uncertain. This paper introduces a novel, distributed protocol that enables multiple IoT devices to perform OTA updates via CT simultaneously. We provide a formal analysis of the protocol's scalability, reliability, and energy efficiency, alongside a detailed implementation. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach can reduce update durations by a factor of 100 compared to traditional methods, while maintaining reliability rates exceeding 99%.

We investigate the fractal nature of eigenstates and self-energy within the many-body localized (MBL) phase of disordered interacting systems. Our findings reveal that the fractal dimension linked to self-energy is not constant but varies continuously as the system approaches the transition from thermal to MBL states. Additionally, we observe that the fractal dimension of eigenstates in the MBL phase is not uniform across the entire spectrum; instead, it depends on the specific energy density.

This paper introduces the kBalanced-MP Differential Privacy (kBM-DP) algorithm, a novel approach to solving the MultipleTargets problem under a new definition of adaptive robustness. The algorithm operates by maintaining a dynamic data structure that tracks the relative ranks of candidate solutions, allowing it to adaptively select the optimal answer. By utilizing this structure, kBM-DP achieves a computational complexity of $O(\text{poly}(n) \cdot \log(n))$, where $n$ represents the input size, thereby significantly improving upon the efficiency of prior algorithms. Furthermore, the paper establishes a lower bound on the robustness of any algorithm solving MultipleTargets, demonstrating that the achieved upper bound is nearly tight.

Machine learning models are vulnerable to adversarial examples, which are intentionally crafted inputs designed to trigger incorrect predictions. While prior research has extensively examined this weakness in classical systems, the impact on quantum machine learning remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the susceptibility of variational quantum classifiers to such attacks. We demonstrate that adversarial examples successfully deceive these quantum models, yielding erroneous outputs. To address this, we evaluate two defense strategies: one involving the application of a data preprocessing technique to quantum classifiers and another utilizing variational quantum decoders. Our findings indicate that both approaches effectively mitigate the influence of adversarial noise, ensuring the quantum classifier produces accurate predictions.

This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of $l$-Stecklov eigenvalues for domains within $\mathbb{R}^n$ as they approach a limit. We demonstrate that for a sequence of domains $D_k$ converging to a domain $D$ in the Hausdorff-Froliksev sense, the corresponding $l$-Stecklov eigenvalues are lower semicontinuous. Furthermore, we analyze the asymptotics of these eigenvalues for $l$-Stecklov on sequences of ellipsoids and spheres with radii shrinking to zero. We show that if $l$ is not a square integer, the volume-normalized eigenvalues diverge to infinity; if $l$ is a square integer, they converge to a specific finite limit determined by an optimization problem over spherical harmonics.

We introduce a new approach to aligning process executions that treats executions as ordered sequences of transitions, analogous to text represented as sequences of characters. This method extends traditional alignments—which focus solely on matching activity names—to encompass structural elements such as control-flow and data-flow. By representing executions as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), we define three new alignment types: infix, postfix, and divide-and-conquer. These approaches offer a more comprehensive view of execution differences by capturing nuances in execution order, structural composition, and the flow of both control and data. We have developed a tool named "align4j" to compute these alignments, which has been validated through real-world case studies.

Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have proven highly effective in diverse machine learning domains, including image and speech recognition. This study explores their application to radio propagation modeling, specifically addressing the challenge of predicting signal attenuation in urban environments. We propose a novel CNN architecture that learns to map geographic coordinates to attenuation values, achieving results that surpass conventional modeling techniques. Additionally, we examine the network's ability to learn signal attenuation patterns from real-world measurements and assess its generalization capabilities when presented with data from locations outside its training set.

The primary objective of this paper is to investigate how validation algorithms can enhance temporal planning systems. We introduce a novel algorithm for validating temporal plans, which leverages the principles of lazy evaluation and dynamic re-planning. Additionally, we examine the algorithm's performance in the context of validation tasks.

This study examines the impact of temporal resolution on power system models, specifically focusing on capacity expansion and the allocation of generation assets. The analysis centers on the European context, utilizing a high-resolution model with 5,700 nodes and 12,000 time steps to assess the impacts of climate change and the integration of renewables. The research evaluates scenarios spanning from 2020 to 2050, incorporating various technology mixes and policy frameworks. The primary objective is to determine the costs of capacity allocation and their sensitivity to temporal resolution, while also exploring the link between modeling resolution and investment decisions. The findings reveal that temporal resolution significantly influences capacity allocation costs, with coarse models potentially overlooking crucial transmission investments. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that capacity allocation outcomes are highly sensitive to temporal resolution, underscoring the necessity for high-resolution data in power system modeling. This work examines the well-posedness of the three-dimensional Vlasov-Poisson system for both screened and unscreened cases in dimensions one and two, accommodating diverse boundary constraints. Specifically, Dirichlet conditions apply to Poisson's equation, while Neumann conditions are utilized for the Lorentzian variant. The analysis relies on the application of a fixed point theorem, which requires a priori estimates concerning the nonlinear solution of the system.

This paper introduces a novel algorithm designed to identify appropriate search terms for software refactoring activities. It evaluates the terms within the codebase using two distinct metrics: TextRank and POSRank. These measures assess textual relevance based respectively on term co-occurrence frequencies and part-of-speech patterns. The study applies this approach to a collection of 100,000 refactoring tasks, demonstrating that the proposed technique can effectively locate suitable search terms for such activities.

Rheo-acoustic gels are engineered to respond to ultrasound by transitioning between solid and fluid states, a mechanism widely utilized in drug delivery and tissue engineering. While ultrasound-assisted gelation is well-documented, the dynamics of ultrasound-induced gel fluidization remain poorly understood. This study investigates the fluidization dynamics of ultrasound-rheo-acog gels using a novel approach: a high-speed camera coupled with a transparent acoustic window. This setup enables the direct visualization of particle trajectories within the gel, allowing for the calculation of particle velocity and acceleration. The results demonstrate that the resulting fluidization dynamics are governed by acoustic intensity and frequency, as well as the gel's intrinsic rheological properties. Furthermore, we introduce a theoretical framework to model the fluidization process, which aligns well with experimental observations. Ultimately, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of ultrasound-driven gel fluidization, offering a pathway for the development of advanced ultrasound-responsive devices.

This work demonstrates an approach to proving the Collatz conjecture by applying mathematical induction alongside a specific function $f(n)$, which represents the number of iterations required for a given integer $n$ to reach 1 under the Collatz process. The authors establish this function $f(n)$ through strong induction and subsequently employ it within a secondary proof by induction to validate the conjecture itself.

Explainable AI (XAI) is a rapidly growing field dedicated to interpreting the decisions made by machine learning models. While numerous XAI methods exist for image and text classification, few are specifically designed for document classification. This paper introduces a novel approach to document classification that leverages the TF-IDF technique to generate word embeddings, which are subsequently processed by a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). To interpret the model's decisions, we employ the LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation) method. The proposed framework is evaluated on three datasets: the 20 Newsgroups, the R8, and the RC datasets. Results indicate that our model achieves an accuracy of 91.4%, 90.1%, and 92.9% on the respective datasets. Furthermore, LIME analysis demonstrates that the model correctly identifies key words within test documents, confirming the reliability of our explanation method.

Stable matching theory is a cornerstone of matching theory, particularly in large-scale markets where public ratings significantly influence utility. This study investigates the impact of ratings on stable matching markets, specifically examining how rating strategies affect agents' outcomes. We introduce a rating strategy designed to enhance an agent's own utility, demonstrating that this approach benefits the agent not only individually but also improves their final matching result. Furthermore, we prove that this strategy is Pareto optimal for the agent. Our findings are supported by extensive experiments, which validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

This paper introduces SummScore, a new evaluation metric for English summary generation. It surpasses current metrics by offering greater diversity, a stronger alignment with human ratings, and a higher correlation between those ratings and its own scores. SummScore operates by training a classifier to distinguish between human-written and model-generated summaries; the final score is derived from the model's Area Under the Curve (AUC) performance on this classifier. To support this, we release a new dataset comprising 1,000 manually annotated summaries across ten diverse domains, each paired with three human-written variants.

We investigate the maximum level of sparsity recoverable from cross-correlated measurements, specifically focusing on how the number of correlated entries $M$ influences the achievable recovery threshold. Our findings indicate that as $M$ increases, the recoverable sparsity level decreases. We also provide a theoretical bound for the cross-correlated case by adapting techniques originally developed for purely random matrices. Furthermore, we examine the performance of the $\ell_1$ minimization method, demonstrating that it remains effective even in scenarios involving significant amounts of correlated data.

Although LiDAR and monocular cameras are the primary sensors for autonomous driving, their data is often fused at a post-processing level, which limits performance when one sensor fails. To address this, we introduce **BEVFusion**, a novel end-to-end object detection framework that operates entirely within a bird's-eye view (BEV) representation. This architecture leverages the complementary strengths of both cameras and LiDAR to enhance detection accuracy and robustness. Specifically, we employ **BEMoCap** to generate high-quality BEV representations from camera imagery and introduce **LiDAR2BEV** to project raw LiDAR point clouds into the BEV plane. These two modules are integrated into a unified **BESFusion** backbone, which utilizes cross-attention mechanisms to dynamically align and aggregate features from both modalities. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that BEVFusion significantly improves resilience to sensor failures, such as those caused by adverse weather conditions.

The primary focus of this work is the derivation of a fluctuating hydrodynamics equation for incompressible fluids, which incorporates stochastic terms to account for the irreversible entropy production arising from viscous dissipation. We demonstrate that, in the macroscopic limit, this equation converges to the standard deterministic Navier-Stokes equation. However, at the mesoscopic level, fluctuating hydrodynamics provides a more comprehensive description of turbulence, specifically regarding the cascade of energy and its ultimate dissipation. This framework is applied to examine the statistical properties of energy dissipation in both homogeneous isotropic turbulence and near-wall turbulence.

We report on the generation of intricate, self-organized structures within laser diffraction patterns formed by light traversing a fluid heated by a hot plate. This experimental approach offers a straightforward means to investigate the interaction between thermal and optical instabilities. The fluid, a colloidal suspension of polystyrene beads in water, exhibits simultaneous thermal and optical instability, resulting in distinct phenomena. The fluid's diffraction patterns reveal a transition from regular to chaotic turbulence, featuring both a shift in primary wavelength and the emergence of secondary structures. These observations align well with the predictions of linear stability theory and the established results of nonlinear thermal convection.

Although design mining has recently gained traction, it remains a nascent field. This study introduces a new approach to design recommendation that enhances conclusion stability, increases the relevance of findings across different projects, and reduces dependency on manual intervention. Our method leverages a recommendation engine to automatically suggest design modifications, a feature that can be readily integrated into existing design recommendation frameworks. Evaluation results demonstrate that our technique surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both stability and relevance.

Data streams generated by IoT devices often present significant challenges regarding high volume and velocity, posing difficulties for traditional centralized architectures. H-STREAM is proposed as a decentralized, blockchain-based solution designed to overcome these hurdles. By leveraging a peer-to-peer network, the system ensures that data is stored in a tamper-proof manner while maintaining privacy through the use of homomorphic encryption. This encryption allows for the verification of data integrity without exposing the underlying raw information. The system's functionality and security are supported by a specialized consensus mechanism tailored for stream processing, which prioritizes efficiency. The proposed architecture is evaluated through a comprehensive analysis of its security properties and a performance assessment conducted via a dedicated simulation framework.

This study introduces a novel sequence-to-sequence architecture for generating SPARQL queries, employing a copy mechanism to resolve the vocabulary limitation inherent in standard encoder-decoder frameworks. By allowing the model to replicate tokens from the input question rather than relying solely on a fixed vocabulary, we enhanced query generation accuracy. Empirical results indicate that this approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 2.5% relative improvement in recall. Furthermore, we conducted an analysis of copy frequency across different datasets to identify patterns in question phrasing that trigger the copy mechanism.

This paper introduces a novel approach to examining the evolution of research within the computer science domain by leveraging publishing venues. By utilizing venue-level metadata, we can track shifts in publication focus, analyze the growth of specific fields, and map the connections between them. Our methodology involves a comprehensive analysis of the DBLP computer science bibliography, covering the period from 1985 to 2015. Our findings demonstrate that publishing venue data offers valuable insights into the historical progression of computer science research.

This paper introduces a novel framework for verifying the robustness of black-box neural networks within control system contexts. The approach leverages recent advancements in robustness analysis derived from the computer vision and machine learning communities. By employing a black-box gradient-based adversarial attack to generate an approximate robustness certificate, the method effectively addresses challenges inherent to black-box settings, such as the absence of direct gradient access and significant computational costs. The attack process is enhanced by integrating a batch normalization layer into the network architecture, which facilitates more efficient computation. Furthermore, the work extends this methodology to systems with uncertain parameters, offering a solution for robustness analysis in black-box scenarios.

We introduce a broad class of functorial clustering schemes that extend to single-linkage clustering, offering a solution to the well-known failure of the latter in satisfying the dimension constraint. This framework encompasses the schemes proposed by Bickel and others (2013) and Chazal et al. (2014), as well as a novel approach for link clustering based on the Čech complex. We establish the strong consistency of these methods and derive upper bounds for their rates of convergence.

Motion in video sequences poses significant challenges for streaming tensor completion (STC) algorithms, often causing performance degradation. To address this, we introduce a novel STC approach that leverages the inherent sparsity of motion. Our method employs a specialized motion detection technique to identify moving regions, which are then imputed using a new algorithm designed to handle a single missing mode within a low-rank tensor. We further developed an efficient, fast solver for the resulting optimization task. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses existing methods in both accuracy and computational speed.

This paper demonstrates that, except for a few specific instances, Nichols algeores associated with classical Weyl groups are generally infinite-dimensional. We establish this by constructing an explicit, faithful action of a Drinfeld double on a Nichols algebra. This approach extends the method originally proposed by Andruskiw and Van Oystaeyen for the rank 2 case.

This study examines inertial wave turbulence in a laboratory setting, utilizing a rotating, forced, and damped mechanical oscillator. The experimental outcomes confirm a $k^{-7/3}$ spectrum, which aligns with the $k^{-7/3}$ profile predicted analytically by Gohil et al. (2015) and corresponds to the theoretical direct energy cascade. Additionally, the research investigates the influence of anisotropic dissipation on the energy budget, specifically analyzing how dissipation impacts the energy input rate.

Graph normalization is a recently introduced probabilistic framework designed to address the Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) problem. This study establishes a direct link between the iterative graph normalization process and the MWIS problem, specifically demonstrating that the process converges to a solution that maximizes the weighted sum of node degrees. The authors also explore the relationship between graph normalization and the Wulff potential, a concept utilized in optimization for solving the MWIS problem. Furthermore, the paper presents a theoretical analysis of the convergence of the iterative graph normalization process, providing insights into its behavior and effectiveness. We investigate the electronic properties of a graphene layer subjected to a periodic electric field and a perpendicular magnetic field. By employing a semi-classical approach, we derive the Landau Level (LL) oscillations arising from the interference between these two fields. Our findings indicate that both sinusoidal and square-root type behaviors are observed in these oscillations, contingent upon the relative phase of the electric modulation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the extrema of these oscillations are governed by the ratio of the electric modulation amplitude to the magnetic field strength.

This study presents new observations of the M dwarf binary system CR Draconis, conducted using the Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) at 1.4 GHz. The data reveal a complex radio structure characterized by a central core and two extended lobes. The system's emission is notably fainter than that of Jupiter, with a flux density of 0.012 mJy, and exhibits a high degree of linear polarization (60%). Furthermore, the polarized signal displays a distinct circular pattern, suggesting a non-uniform magnetic field geometry. These findings are consistent with a model of non-thermal radiation generated by a population of relativistic electrons within a magnetic field. The study also explores the potential influence of the companion star on the emission characteristics of CR Draconis.

Current Articulated Neural Rendering (AR) frameworks typically rely on pre-trained neural radiance fields (NeRFs) for individual object parts, which are then combined via volume rendering. However, this approach suffers from two main drawbacks: it cannot render moving parts, and it struggles with occlusion handling. To address these limitations, we introduce a new framework that models the world volume as a function of both spatial coordinates and part-specific semantics. By utilizing a Part-aware Query Transformer, we learn to segment a scene into distinct parts, each associated with a specific neural rendering function. This allows for the direct synthesis of neural representations for arbitrary object parts within a scene. Consequently, our method enables articulated rendering of dynamic scenes, including the handling of self-occlusion and inter-part occlusion. We validate our approach on both simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods.

Artificial neural networks often fail to match human visual capabilities when it comes to recognizing objects under extreme distortions. This study investigates the link between human and machine recognition performance by analyzing how both systems handle severely warped images. We introduce a novel distortion metric based on the entropy of the warped image's power spectrum to quantify these perturbations. Our findings indicate that while humans can recognize categories in images distorted beyond the threshold of artificial networks, this ability is constrained by both the degree of distortion and the specific object category.

We demonstrate that specific Wilson loops in Chern-Simons theory correspond to the generators of the Askey-Wilson algebra. This correspondence enables the derivation of closed-form expressions for these loops by leveraging known properties of the algebra. Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations are widely used to study strongly correlated systems, yet the sign problem often restricts their application to regimes where simulations remain feasible only at high temperatures. This study demonstrates that by employing a trimer-based computational basis, the QMC sign problem can be significantly mitigated, enabling simulations at much lower temperatures. This approach is applied to the two-dimensional $J$-$J'$ Heisenberg model, a system exhibiting complex phase diagrams, including spin dimers, spiral, and stripe orders. Our findings indicate that the proposed basis offers a substantial reduction in the sign problem compared to both the standard and previously proposed triangular basis sets.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success across numerous NLP tasks, with zero-shot learning (ZSL) emerging as a particularly promising application. This study investigates the relationship between PLM scale and ZSL performance by analyzing GPT-2 models ranging from 124 million to 1.5 billion parameters. We evaluate these models on a broad spectrum of 1,000 Wikipedia-based datasets covering 34 distinct categories, encompassing tasks such as sentiment analysis, question answering, and entity linking. Our findings reveal a clear positive correlation: larger models consistently achieve superior AUC-ROC scores compared to smaller counterparts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fine-tuning yields substantial performance gains for both scales, yet the magnitude of improvement is notably greater for the larger model.

We examine the viability of a strong first-order electroweak phase transition within the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) by employing the tree-level approximation for the phase transition dynamics. Our analysis focuses on two critical constraints: the latest LHC searches regarding Higgs boson decays into bottom quarks and the stringent bounds on the Higgs-to-dilaton decay rate derived from the Higgs-to-dilaton channel. We find that these experimental constraints significantly restrict the parameter space associated with a strong first-order phase transition. Specifically, these constraints are most severe in scenarios where the dilaton is light, as such regions are largely excluded.

The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) is a highly capable instrument for identifying galaxies at redshifts exceeding 2, offering the ability to measure reliable redshifts up to $z \approx 4$ using spectral energy distribution (SED) photometry. This study evaluates the ALMA capacity for obtaining robust redshifts within the $2 < z < 4$ range by analyzing 1000 simulated galaxy samples across various redshifts, stellar mass levels, and dust extinction scenarios. We assess the reliability of these redshifts based on the number of ALMA-detected emission lines and continuum peaks, as well as the accuracy of the resulting redshift estimates. Our findings indicate that ALMA can secure robust redshifts for approximately 70% of galaxies with stellar masses exceeding $10^{10} M_\odot$ at $z > 2$. Furthermore, for a fixed stellar mass, the fraction of successfully recovered redshifts diminishes as dust extinction increases.

We demonstrate that low-lying monopole excitations in U(1) gauge theories are directly linked to Dirac spin liquid phases. Specifically, the Dirac mass gap separating the spin liquid from a phase featuring a U(1) symmetry breaking condensate is proportional to the mass of the lowest-lying monopole. This finding is supported by numerical calculations on 4D lattices for both the compact and extended Schwinger models, as well as the 4D toric code.

We investigate the explicit $Z_3$ symmetry breaking in one-dimensional bosonic systems with a single optical lattice site per atom, utilizing a time-dependent mean-field approach. Our results indicate that increasing the number of temporal lattice sites significantly amplifies the breaking strength, a trend that is further enhanced by a higher number of spatial lattice sites. Additionally, we observe that the breaking magnitude grows with increasing interaction strength and diminishes as the system's energy increases.

This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the magnetic characteristics of the L1$_0$-ordered Cr$_2$Al alloy. Results indicate that Cr$_2$Al exhibits antiferromagnetic ordering along the [110] direction, contrasting with the ferromagnetic order seen in Mn$_2$Au. Furthermore, the material displays a substantial anomalous Hall effect, driven by both the anomalous and ordinary components of the Hall resistivity. The anomalous Hall resistivity arises from Berry curvature, while the ordinary component stems from the Lorentz force. Notably, Cr$_2$As exhibits a significantly higher anomalous Hall coefficient than Cr$_2$Al, attributed to the former's larger Berry curvature.

This study introduces a novel $
u$-model for simulating canonical rarefied micro-flows, specifically focusing on thermal transpiration. We evaluate the $
u$-model against the standard Maxwell-Boltzmann (MB) model by examining a thermal transpiration scenario involving two isothermal parallel plates subjected to a temperature differential. Results indicate that the $
u$-model accurately captures the flow behavior across the entire Knudsen spectrum, whereas the MB model fails to do so. Furthermore, the thermal transpiration velocity predicted by the $
u$-model aligns with both analytical solutions and experimental data.

This study introduces a new approach to enhance few-shot semantic parsing by leveraging large language models (LLMs) to generate synthetic data from unlabeled resources. We introduce a methodology designed to create high-quality task-specific training data, which is then utilized to fine-tune an LLM-based semantic parser. Our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 10.4% absolute improvement in F1 score on the TACO dataset and a 12.9% absolute improvement on the TALLAQI dataset.

The European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) is advancing the design of tracking detectors for the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) to meet the stringent demands of the HL-LHC era. This project involves the development of new sensor technologies, including the Depleted Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor (DMAPS) and the AC-coupled Low Gain Avalanche Diode (AC-LGAD). These innovations are designed to enhance tracking capabilities and enable the integration of sensor readout with front-end electronics. This paper presents the results of a comparative study evaluating the performance of DMAPS and AC-LGAD sensors using a 25 GeV proton beam at the CERN SPS. The analysis covers sensor response, spatial resolution, and the performance of the ALICE 3 prototype detector, which incorporates these new sensor technologies.

This study presents the most comprehensive multi-epoch X-ray analysis of the low-mass AGN 2XMM J123103.2+110648, utilizing data from XMM-Newton, Swift, and NuSTAR collected between 2007 and 2021. The source exhibits a complex variability pattern characterized by significant changes in both flux and spectral shape. Specifically, the AGN displayed hard spectral states in 2007 and 2011, followed by a soft state in 2012, and returned to a hard state in 2016. Notably, the 2016 observation recorded the highest flux level to date, with a peak luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^{42}$ erg s$^{-1}$ at 2 keV. Spectral fitting using a simple absorbed power-law model yielded photon indices of $\Gamma = 1.7$–$1.8$ across most epochs, except for 2012, where $\Gamma = 2.4$. Furthermore, spectral curvature was detected in 2012 and 2016, with the latter showing a hardening trend at higher energies. The 2016 NuSTAR data revealed a photon index of $\Gamma = 1.7$ extending up to 100 keV, indicating a lack of spectral cutoff.

The discovery of magnetospheres around B-type magnetic stars has prompted speculation regarding their origins. This study reports the detection of H$\alpha$ emission in the B0.5 V star HD 160617, a system known for its strong magnetic field. The emission line exhibits significant variability in both intensity and equivalent width, with a periodicity of approximately 1.5 days that aligns with the star's rotation. The observed variability suggests a non-uniform distribution of magnetospheric plasma. Furthermore, the study notes the presence of a weak, low-frequency periodicity of roughly 10 days in the H$\alpha$ data. This secondary signal may indicate the presence of a close companion in a 10-day orbit, potentially explaining the star's anomalous rotational behavior.

In one dimension, oscillator operators are linked to intertwining operators through the concept of the "distinguished" oscillator. In higher dimensions, this relationship is established by defining a set of intertwining operators derived from the "distinguished" oscillator set. These findings are illustrated using the examples of the harmonic oscillator and the isotropic harmonic oscillator.

We have conducted a systematic study of the star formation rate (SFR) in low-metallicity starburst galaxies by comparing SFRs derived from total infrared (IR) flux with those obtained from H$\alpha$ and H30$\alpha$ emission lines. Utilizing a sample of 12 galaxies with metallicities below 0.5 times solar, we found that SFRs calculated from total IR flux are generally lower than those derived from H30$\alpha$ lines. This discrepancy is attributed to the fact that the total IR SFR relies on a fixed conversion factor, which fails to account for the variable fraction of young stars obscured by dust. In contrast, the H30$\alpha$-based SFRs incorporate dust-corrected line luminosities, making them more accurate for these systems. Consequently, the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a more reliable tracer of star formation in low-metallicity starburst galaxies compared to total IR flux.

This paper examines the continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on topological spaces, specifically focusing on the coarse and uniformly coarse categories. We demonstrate that while some virtually cyclic groups exhibit properties distinct from the infinite dihedral group—such as admitting uniform actions with arbitrarily small open sets that are invariant under the group action—these groups still differ fundamentally in how their dynamics behave globally. However, our analysis reveals that for the infinite dihedral group, any uniformly coarse minimal action possesses a unique characteristic: there exists a canonical homeomorphism between the associated Čech-Stone compactification and the Stone-Čech compactification of the group itself, which is not true for all virtually cyclic groups. This distinction underscores the special role the infinite dihedral group plays within the class of virtually cyclic groups, particularly regarding the rigidity of its dynamics in the coarse category.

This study examines the application of kernel-based methods in solving stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) and contrasts them with traditional projection methods, such as Galerkin techniques. We introduce a new class of SPDE solvers that utilize conditional expectations derived from specific kernel-based Monte Carlo integration methods. By employing a variational framework, we establish the convergence of these kernel-based approaches and demonstrate that their convergence rates align with those of standard Monte Carlo techniques. Furthermore, we prove that the approximation error of our method is comparable to that of classical Monte Carlo approaches. The proposed algorithm is validated through numerical experiments on a high-dimensional option pricing problem, where results indicate that kernel-based techniques can achieve similar accuracy to classical methods using significantly fewer basis functions.

This paper introduces a novel observer architecture designed for nonlinear systems, including the widely used sliding mode observer (SMO). The proposed design ensures that state estimation errors converge to a specific neighborhood of the true values within a guaranteed finite time. The architecture comprises two primary components: a finite-time convergent reduced-order observer (RCO) and a finite-time non-smooth term (NST). The RC O utilizes a subset of system outputs to estimate the full state vector in finite time, while the NST is constructed from measured outputs and their derivatives to address unmeasured dynamics. The RC O generates a state estimate for a single output, which is then differentiated to produce the NST input. This architecture is applied to a deterministic epidemic model to demonstrate its efficacy. The proposed observer was compared against two standard approaches: the standard SMO and a full-order RCO. Simulation results indicate that the proposed observer offers superior performance by achieving higher accuracy and greater robustness against measurement noise compared to both alternatives.

This paper introduces a new approach to enhancing temporal knowledge graph embeddings by leveraging time-aware metapaths. We posit that utilizing these structures allows for the aggregation of information from various distances within the graph, thereby enriching representations with valuable contextual cues. Our proposed framework, Temporal Metapath Attention Networks (TempMAT), learns time-aware metapath embeddings and employs a attention mechanism to integrate features from different metapath levels. Evaluated on three standard benchmarks, TempMAT outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, including those that use self-supervised learning. Furthermore, a case study demonstrates the practical value of our model by uncovering meaningful relationships between entities and time.

Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLML) is a highly effective method for generating ultrashort pulses, yet it demands precise tuning of numerous parameters, making it difficult to master. This study introduces a straightforward and reliable approach to Kerr-lens mode-locking that requires no trial-and-error tuning. The system operates by inserting a single intracavity etalon, which is optimized for optimal performance through a specific thick-glass lens placed just before the modulator. This method was validated using a Ti:SAP laser, producing stable 100-fs pulses with 3.5 J of energy at a 100 Hz repetition rate.

Federated learning (FL) is a machine learning framework designed to train models across distributed devices while preserving data privacy. In asynchronous FL, participants train locally and submit updates at varying times, introducing communication bottlenecks that delay convergence. This study demonstrates that partial-sharing-based communication can mitigate these delays. By having participants share only a subset of their model parameters, FL can achieve convergence at a rate comparable to fully-sharing methods but with significantly fewer communication rounds. This approach is particularly effective in scenarios involving numerous small-scale clients, such as smartphones, where bandwidth constraints are critical.

This study examines the optical absorption in a thin silicon layer backed by a silicon photonic crystal (PhC) mirror. The PhC structure features a triangular lattice of air holes, and the analysis utilizes plane-wave expansion to calculate the PhC's reflectance spectrum, which is then integrated into a transfer-matrix model to determine the film's total absorption. Results indicate that absorption is highly dependent on the PhC geometry and silicon film thickness. Specifically, absorption peaks occur at wavelengths corresponding to the PhC's reflection band edges. By optimizing the structure, the PhC mirror can boost absorption in a 100 nm silicon film to 90% at 1.55 µm, a significant 40% increase over the 50% absorption achieved with a standard metal reflector.

We introduce two novel functions, $f_1$ and $f_2$, that extend the domain of the exponential map within the complex plane and exhibit specific invariance properties under these functions. Their construction is motivated by the dynamics of the exponential map, and they are designed to fill gaps left by previously known entire functions with similar periodicity and orbit conjugacy. This study explores their geometric structures, including fundamental domains, and investigates the behavior of orbits, particularly focusing on escaping behavior and the existence of Baker domains. Additionally, we analyze Julia sets, providing insights into how these new functions interact with classical examples while revealing unique dynamical features.

High-dimensional expanders are a burgeoning field with promising applications in derandomization, quantum computing, and error-correcting codes. This paper introduces a novel class of expanders constructed from random graphs, characterized by a specific link structure. We demonstrate that when this structure is satisfied by the 2-skeletons of regular polyhedral cell complexes, the resulting expanders achieve linear time quantum vertex recovery from a fraction of faulty vertices. Furthermore, we establish that the random link expansion of these complexes follows a semircircle law distribution in their spectrum.

The magnetic properties of this material were investigated using neutron powder diffraction, revealing that the moments align antiferromagnetically along the $c$-axis with partial antiparallel ordering on the $ab$-plane. Graph representation learning has become a vital tool for analyzing large-scale networks, yet existing methods often fail to effectively capture the influence of a node's neighbors, particularly in sparse networks. This study introduces a novel approach to node representation using the Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM), which incorporates spectral graph theory to derive a node influence matrix. This matrix quantifies how a node impacts its neighbors up to a specified distance $k$. We propose a new learning framework, SNHAM-Learner, designed to derive low-dimensional node embeddings by integrating this influence matrix with a random-walk-based algorithm. Empirical results demonstrate that SNHAM-Learner outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in embedding quality, especially within sparse networks.

This study investigates the activation of a vapor-phase explosive, specifically 1,3,5-trinitro-1,3,5-triazinane (RDX), utilizing a two-chamber structure. This geometry offers a distinct advantage by maintaining a high RDX vapor density within the secondary chamber, thereby preventing premature reactions before the material reaches the initiation source. The research focuses on the interaction between a laser pulse and the target in the primary chamber, specifically examining how the laser couples with a water-based medium to generate a shock wave that propagates into the secondary chamber. The study analyzes the resulting pressure waves and shock fronts using a one-dimensional hydrodynamic model, with key parameters such as pressure, shock velocity, and vapor density calculated and visualized. The findings indicate that the activation process is governed by the interplay between the laser's energy deposition and the target's material properties. Ultimately, the study provides valuable insights into the complex mechanisms driving the activation of vapor-phase explosives.

Nonlinear interference (NLI) models offer a practical means to assess the impact of nonlinearities in optical systems, particularly benefiting the design of next-generation coherent networks. This paper introduces a generalized NLI framework that applies to any linear time-invariant system, encompassing both single- and multi-channel scenarios. The approach derives the NLI by separating it from the signal and noise, utilizing the fourth-order moment of the noise to quantify the former. The discussion covers the implementation of this model for various scenarios, including the implementation of a fourth-order Volterra series for the fiber nonlinearity kernel. The methodology is then extended to handle more intricate nonlinear kernels, such as those found in highly nonlinear fibers and multi-span configurations. Furthermore, the work demonstrates the application of this generalized framework to standard NLI models, specifically the Gaussian Noise Model (GNM) and the GNM with memory (GNM-M).

This study evaluates the efficacy of deep learning-based image fusion for satellite fire detection by comparing it with traditional fusion techniques. Using the TNO Fire dataset, we trained a deep learning model to generate a synthetic fusion of Visible and Infrared bands, which was then utilized for fire imagery analysis. Our findings indicate that the deep learning approach yields superior results, achieving lower false-positive rates and higher accuracy than conventional fusion methods.

Social media platforms have become integral to modern life, generating vast amounts of data that can potentially aid in diagnosing mental health conditions. This study presents a social media-based framework for detecting depression and anxiety, utilizing a two-stage pipeline. Initially, a two-tiered data preprocessing approach filters and cleans user posts to enhance the quality of input for subsequent analysis. Following this, two distinct classification models are developed to identify depression. The research evaluates these models using two datasets: one containing 1,000 posts from Twitter and another comprising 500 posts from Facebook. Results indicate that the system's performance in diagnosing mental states via social media content rivals that of conventional physical exams. Furthermore, the study analyzes the impact of demographic variables—including age, gender, and education level—on diagnostic accuracy.

The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has prompted numerous studies on the role of hospitals and healthcare institutes in epidemic control. This paper employs a deterministic SEIR model enhanced with a fractional derivative to examine the impact of these institutions alongside lockdown measures. We introduce a new approach to model hospitalization rates, incorporating a control variable that represents the capacity of institutes to isolate infected individuals. By utilizing a control-theory framework, we demonstrate that combining hospitalization and institute-based treatments with lockdowns yields superior outcomes compared to implementing these actions independently. Furthermore, we establish that these control measures are effective only when the pandemic is in its early stages; once it has advanced, they lose their ability to halt transmission.

The study investigates the impact of isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) and Giant Quadrupole Resonance (ISGQR) coupling on the energy structure of the ISGMR within deformed nuclei. Utilizing the Quasi-Boson Approximation (QBA) alongside the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) in a harmonic oscillator basis, the analysis reveals that the ISGMR-Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance (ISGQR) coupling significantly alters the ISGMR energy, a finding that aligns with prior studies on spherical nuclei. The study further examines the influence of this coupling on the energy shift of the ISGMR in both prolate and oblate deformed systems. Results indicate that the ISGMR energy shift is more pronounced in oblate nuclei than in prolate ones. Additionally, the research explores the effects of varying oscillator parameters on the ISGMR energy shift across different deformation conditions.

This study examines a feedback-controlled mass-spring system incorporating stiction, where the control input switches between two constant values outside a specific deadband, inducing the stiction phenomenon. This phenomenon restricts motion whenever the system's velocity falls within the stiction region. The paper establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for ensuring the system's asymptotic stability. Furthermore, it outlines a method to compute the ultimate boundedness of a specific physical quantity, which represents the size of a particular region in the system's state space.

This study examines the impact of trading frictions—including costs and liquidity constraints—on optimal trading strategies and asset pricing. We develop a closed-form solution for an optimal trading policy within a framework featuring both stochastic volatility and interest rates. Additionally, we introduce a novel market-wide stochastic state variable to enhance the empirical relevance of our volatility model. By utilizing actual market data, we evaluate the performance of our proposed policy and compare it against standard benchmark strategies.

Although recommender systems have become a standard method for delivering personalized content, they often overlook user intent, which is crucial for optimizing the experience. To address this gap, this paper introduces a novel approach to modeling user intent by leveraging the semantic relationships between users and items. We introduce a new architecture, the Semantic Graph Attention Network (SGATN), which integrates a semantic graph alongside the traditional user-item interaction graph. This dual-graph structure enables the model to capture intent signals from both explicit interactions and implicit semantic knowledge. Empirical evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate that SGATN outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in predictive accuracy. Furthermore, we validate the approach's effectiveness for intent prediction and its ability to enhance overall user experience.

The double confluent Heun equation, characterized by two finite singularities and one point at infinity, is classified as reducible when its solution space at infinity shrinks from a dimension of two to one. This reduction occurs under specific conditions where the associated Riemann-Hilbert problem admits a solution. In this study, we examine the specific case of a reducible equation, demonstrating that it possesses a holomorphic solution across the entire complex plane excluding the origin if and only if its parameters satisfy a specific quadratic relation. Furthermore, we derive the explicit form of this holomorphic solution and determine the behavior of its associated Heun function as the argument approaches the origin.

This paper investigates the efficacy of principal component analysis (PCA) in recovering low-rank matrices from data corrupted by an arbitrary number of outliers. We establish that when PCA is applied to a weighted combination of the available data combinations, where each weight is a function of the corresponding sample, the resulting estimator achieves optimal minimax rates for both uniform and non-uniform data distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this methodological framework encompasses several prominent outlier-robust techniques, including trimmed least squares, geometric median regression, and Huber regression.

Topological phases in fermionic systems are typically defined by symmetry-protected fractional boundary states. In contrast, this study demonstrates that classical systems can host such states even without time-reversal symmetry. We identify a class of classical systems that can be mapped to free fermions via a Schur-Wiefer-type transformation, thereby allowing us to determine their fractional boundary characteristics using an effective fermionic description. Furthermore, we outline a general strategy for constructing these fractional boundary states in arbitrary dimensions.
